source.title: Recovery of Force–Time Characteristics After Australian Rules Football Matches: Examining the Utility of the Isometric Midthigh Pull

paper.citation: Norris D., Joyce D., Siegler J., Clock J., Lovell R. Recovery of Force–Time Characteristics After Australian Rules Football Matches: Examining the Utility of the Isometric Midthigh Pull. International Journal of Sports Physiology and Performance. 2019;14(6):765-770. doi:10.1123/ijspp.2018-0349.
paper.abstract: This paper addresses the following question: Do IMTP peak force and rate-of-force-development metrics show different recovery patterns and between-match variability after elite Australian rules football competition? Eight elite national-competition Australian rules football players from several positions were observed after three in-season matches. Sixty of 72 planned IMTP samples were collected, and average game time was 106 minutes. This was a repeated-measures observational study. Two rested baseline sessions preceded postmatch testing at 48, 72, and 96 hours.
paper.tldr: RFD from 0–50 ms was reduced relative to baseline at 48, 72, and 96 hours by 25.8%, 17.8%, and 16.9%, respectively. RFD from 100–200 ms was reduced at 48 and 72 hours by 15.7% and 11.7%, while its 96-hour change was classified as trivial. Peak force alone may miss postcompetition changes visible in force-development rate, but early RFD is sensitive to contraction-onset detection and has substantial measurement noise.
paper.methods: This was a repeated-measures observational study. Two rested baseline sessions preceded postmatch testing at 48, 72, and 96 hours. Players performed standardized IMTP trials on dual force plates sampled at 1,000 Hz. Outcomes were peak force, RFD from 0–50 ms, and RFD from 100–200 ms. Mixed-effects models accounted for repeated player and match observations, and changes were classified against study-defined smallest worthwhile changes.
paper.findings: RFD from 0–50 ms was reduced relative to baseline at 48, 72, and 96 hours by 25.8%, 17.8%, and 16.9%, respectively. RFD from 100–200 ms was reduced at 48 and 72 hours by 15.7% and 11.7%, while its 96-hour change was classified as trivial. Peak-force changes were classified as trivial at all three postmatch time points. Baseline coefficient of variation was 16.4% for 0–50-ms RFD, 12.2% for 100–200-ms RFD, and 4.8% for peak force, showing that the more responsive metrics were also noisier. Between-match variability was higher for 0–50-ms RFD than for 100–200-ms RFD or peak force at each reported postmatch time point.
paper.limitations: Only eight players and three matches contributed data, 17% of planned observations were missing, and no immediate or 24-hour assessments were collected. The classification used magnitude-based inference with 90% intervals and study-specific smallest-worthwhile-change rules, so the labels should not be treated as conventional hypothesis-test results. Australian rules football differs from collegiate American football in match structure, collision distribution, running demands, and weekly schedule. The study demonstrates metric behavior, not that IMTP-guided decisions improve performance or reduce injury.
paper.practicalImplications: Peak force alone may miss postcompetition changes visible in force-development rate, but early RFD is sensitive to contraction-onset detection and has substantial measurement noise. If IMTP is used operationally, standardize posture, pretension, instruction, onset processing, testing time, and athlete readiness. Favor within-athlete baselines and confidence bands over single cut points, and interpret RFD alongside exposure, soreness, wellness, and performance. The 100–200-ms window may offer a better sensitivity–reliability compromise in this dataset, but it requires local reliability testing before adoption.

Apply the finding within the population and setting described in the source rather than treating it as a universal threshold.
paper.rtp: The paper did not validate a rehabilitation or return-to-sport decision rule. Its findings may inform supporting training or monitoring during reconditioning, but it provides no standalone clearance threshold or progression criterion.
